strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: making visual prompt tuning interpretable through image-grounded concepts. Combining region-conditioned prompts with hierarchical grouping provides a coherent approach to this goal.

Table 1 evaluates five backbones and includes conventional prototype networks, prompt-tuning methods, and prototype-augmented prompt baselines. IVPT achieves the highest classification accuracy and stability across all five backbones. On DINOv2-B, it reaches 75.3 consistency, 75.9 stability, and 90.8% accuracy.

The cumulative ablation supports the usefulness of region aggregation, hierarchical prototypes, and prompt fusion. Visualizations illustrate recognizable regions in birds, cars, and pathology images, with part annotations withheld during training.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim exceeds the evidence. Consistency and stability measure localization agreement and robustness, not whether the highlighted regions faithfully explain predictions. Patch embeddings already contain contextual information, and subsequent Transformer attention can mix information across regions and prompts. Consequently, averaging concept-head outputs in Equation 6 does not establish region-specific attribution. Concept interventions, deletion tests, or other faithfulness evaluations are needed.

The mathematical specification leaves consequential issues unresolved. Equation 7 adds unconstrained spatial biases after softmax, so attention values need not remain valid probabilities. Equation 12 applies KL divergence to hard-masked region maps without specifying normalization or smoothing; mismatched supports can produce infinite divergence. Equations 10 and 11 also require handling empty regions and groups. These omissions make the actual training objective and its numerical behavior difficult to assess.

Novelty is insufficiently separated from closely related part-discovery methods. The approach explicitly borrows the part-shaping objective from PDiscoFormer, but does not compare against that method or a straightforward integration of it with prompt tuning. The characterization of earlier approaches as lacking cross-category prototype sharing also overlooks related work such as ProtoPShare and ProtoPool. The hierarchical prompt integration is promising, but its incremental contribution needs sharper positioning.

Quantitative evaluation is restricted to CUB-200-2011. Stanford Cars and Gleason-2019 provide only selected visualizations, without classification results, quantitative concept validation, or expert assessment of the pathology interpretations. These examples do not substantiate broad claims about performance across benchmarks or support for diagnostic workflows.

Comparison protocols and reproducibility are underspecified in the supplied manuscript. It omits optimizer settings, training schedules, seed counts, and important implementation details, referring instead to unavailable supplementary material. It also does not adequately explain how conventional prototype networks are adapted to each Transformer backbone or how ordinary prompt tokens are converted into regions for the interpretability metrics. Trainable parameter counts and computational costs are absent.

The ablations do not isolate hierarchy from additional capacity, supervision, and prompt placement. Missing controls include matched-capacity flat prototypes, removal of the consistency loss, and alternatives to learned grouping. Interpretability is measured at the second-to-last layer with ten concepts, whereas classification uses four final prompts, leaving the quality of the actual decision-level hierarchy insufficiently tested. Accuracy gains over the strongest baselines are only 0.3–0.9 percentage points, with no repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: making visual prompt tuning interpretable through image-grounded concepts. Combining region-based prompt generation with hierarchical concept alignment is a promising direction.

Table 1 provides comparisons across five backbones, including conventional prototype networks, prompt-tuning methods, and prototype-enhanced prompt baselines. IVPT achieves the highest reported accuracy and stability on every backbone.
The cumulative ablation provides positive evidence for the proposed components: on DINOv2-B, consistency improves from 62.7 to 75.3 and accuracy from 88.4% to 90.8%.
Concept discovery uses image-level supervision without training-time part annotations, and the visualizations illustrate recognizable regions across birds, cars, and pathology images.
weaknesses: The central claim of faithful interpretability is insufficiently established. Region aggregation uses contextualized Transformer features, and subsequent self-attention can mix information across regions. Consequently, a localized region map does not establish that its corresponding prediction contribution depends on that region. Consistency and stability measure localization properties, but no concept interventions, region-removal experiments, or information-leakage analysis validate the claimed explanations.

Important mathematical details are unresolved. Equation 7 adds an unconstrained bias after softmax, contradicting the stated probability bounds. Equation 12 applies KL divergence to hard-masked maps without specifying normalization or smoothing; mismatched supports can produce infinite divergence. Equations 10 and 11 also require handling empty regions or groups, which is not described.

Novelty relative to closely related part-discovery approaches is insufficiently isolated. The region-discovery mechanism and part-shaping losses explicitly build on PDiscoFormer, yet this method is absent from the comparisons. A matched part-discovery baseline with the same backbone and classification head is needed to establish the benefit of hierarchical prompting.

Quantitative evaluation is restricted to CUB-200-2011. Cars and pathology provide only qualitative examples in the supplied manuscript, so claims of comprehensive cross-domain effectiveness and diagnostic relevance exceed the demonstrated evidence. Clinical concept labels are not validated through quantitative annotations or expert assessment.

Interpretability is evaluated using ten concepts from the second-to-last layer, whereas classification uses four final concepts. The paper does not quantitatively establish the semantic consistency or attribution faithfulness of these actual decision-level concepts. Equation 6 also does not explain how the normalized importance values in Figure 4 are obtained.

Reproducibility and experimental controls are incomplete in the supplied manuscript, which refers to unavailable supplementary material. Training settings, baseline adaptation details, perturbation protocols, parameter counts, and computational costs are not sufficiently documented. There are no repeated-run uncertainties, and accuracy gains over the strongest prototype-enhanced prompt baselines are only 0.3–0.5 percentage points on four backbones.

The cumulative ablation does not separate hierarchy from additional capacity, layer placement, or the consistency loss. Comparisons against equal-sized nonhierarchical prompts and independent removal of each component would strengthen attribution of the gains. Overall, the promising results do not yet resolve the methodological and evidential gaps required for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: making visual prompts interpretable through image-grounded concepts. Combining region-based prompt generation with cross-layer concept grouping is a coherent and potentially useful contribution.

The reported evaluation covers five backbones on CUB and additional quantitative results on PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part. IVPT generally improves interpretability metrics while maintaining or improving classification accuracy.

Prototype-augmented prompt baselines and component ablations provide useful evidence beyond comparisons with vanilla VPT. For DinoV2-B, adding cross-layer fusion improves consistency from 70.4 to 75.3 and stability from 70.9 to 75.9.
The visualizations illustrate concepts at different granularities, and the appendix acknowledges meaningful failure cases involving background shortcuts and ambiguous object parts.
weaknesses: The central claim of faithful interpretation is insufficiently supported. Region pooling uses contextualized Transformer features, which can contain information from outside the highlighted region; subsequent attention can further mix concepts. Consequently, localized maps and per-concept classifier scores do not establish that predictions depend on the depicted semantic concepts. Concept interventions, region deletion, or other faithfulness tests are missing, and Equation 4 does not specify how its class-score vectors become the normalized importance values in Figure 5.

The mathematical specification has consequential unresolved issues. Equation 5 adds an unconstrained spatial bias after softmax, so attention values need not remain nonnegative, normalized, or within the stated range. This conflicts with their use as probabilities and with the entropy loss. Equation 8 applies KL divergence to hard-masked region maps without specifying normalization or smoothing; differing supports can yield infinite divergence. Equation 7 also requires an unspecified safeguard for empty regions.

Comparisons omit particularly relevant methods. PDiscoFormer supplies the part-discovery machinery and regularizers but is not evaluated directly, and Prompt-CAM is discussed without an experimental comparison. Moreover, the blanket characterization of prior prototypes as class-specific overlooks prototype-sharing approaches, including cited ProtoPool and ProtoPShare. These omissions weaken both the novelty positioning and attribution of gains to interpretable prompting.

Evaluation protocols are not sufficiently specified to establish fair, reproducible comparisons. The paper does not adequately explain how conventional prototype networks are adapted to the Transformer backbones or how prompt-only methods produce maps for the interpretability metrics. PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part lack clear split, task-construction, and part-matching details. Main results have no repeated-run uncertainty, despite accuracy margins as small as 0.3–0.5 percentage points. Cumulative ablations also leave the individual contributions of regularization, additional capacity, and hierarchy incompletely separated.

The human study is not rigorous enough to substantiate its strong conclusions. The reported 97.5% accuracy depends on matching descriptions to unspecified 'prototype intentions'; the reference labels, scoring procedure, image selection, participant expertise, and inter-rater agreement are absent. There is no baseline or blinded comparison. Similarly, near-perfect cross-layer IoU measures agreement between model-generated regions explicitly trained to agree, rather than independently demonstrating semantic correctness.

Parameter efficiency and reproducibility are incompletely documented. Appendix C counts prototypes and spatial biases but omits trainable fusion/grouping layers, classification heads, and unfrozen backbone tokens and positional embeddings. Appendix A's unfrozen parameters also qualify the main text's claim that only prompt embeddings are updated. Full parameter totals, MLP dimensions, and reproducible timing conditions are needed; the abstract's promised code link is blank.

Several broader conclusions exceed the evidence. Qualitative examples and separately fine-tuned domain models do not establish robustness to unseen domain shifts. The pathology claims lack expert validation and quantitative diagnostic evaluation; Appendix F's assertion that glandular lumen has no direct relevance to cancer is particularly problematic because glandular architecture and lumen formation are relevant to Gleason grading.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: making visual prompts interpretable through spatially grounded concepts and relationships across network layers.

Reports encouraging results across five backbones on CUB and additional quantitative evaluations on PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part. On CUB with DINOv2-B, IVPT achieves 90.8% accuracy versus 89.1% for VPT-Deep, alongside improved consistency and stability.

Includes prototype-augmented prompting baselines, component and prototype-count ablations, qualitative examples, and failure cases. These provide useful evidence that the proposed combination merits further investigation.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification has consequential unresolved issues. Equation 5 adds an unconstrained spatial bias after softmax, invalidating the stated probability bounds and potentially the logarithmic losses. Equation 8 applies KL divergence to unnormalized, hard-masked region maps with potentially incompatible zero supports; normalization and smoothing are unspecified. Equation 7 also lacks handling for empty regions. These omissions prevent confident assessment of the implemented objective.

Spatial grounding does not establish faithful explanation of predictions. Patch embeddings already contain information mixed through global attention, and prompts undergo further processing. Consequently, a region-pooled prompt need not represent only its highlighted region. Equation 4 supplies concept-conditioned classifier scores, but their conversion into the normalized importance values in Figure 5 is unspecified. No intervention, deletion, or concept-editing experiments validate the claimed explanatory importance.

Novelty is insufficiently established against the closest work. The method adopts part discovery machinery and losses from PDiscoFormer, but does not compare directly against it. Prompt-CAM is discussed but omitted from experiments. The blanket characterization of earlier prototypes as class-specific also overlooks the shared-prototype motivation of cited ProtoPool and ProtoPShare. These gaps weaken the claim of a first interpretable VPT paradigm.

Evaluation protocols are insufficiently specified for reliable comparison. The manuscript does not adequately explain how ordinary VPT prompts produce region maps for consistency and stability evaluation, or how prototype baselines are adapted and trained comparably. PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part lack detailed splits and part-to-point evaluation rules. Main results have no repeated-run uncertainty, despite several accuracy gains being only a few tenths of a percentage point.

The evidence for semantic hierarchy and human interpretability is weaker than claimed. The approximately 99% cross-layer IoU measures agreement explicitly encouraged by the training objective, rather than independently establishing meaningful semantic abstraction. The 20-participant study does not specify how 'prototype intentions' are defined or free descriptions scored, and omits baseline comparisons, sampling details, inter-rater agreement, and uncertainty. Its 97.5% accuracy therefore cannot be interpreted confidently.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting are incomplete. Appendix A unfreezes positional embeddings and several backbone tokens despite the main text stating that only prompts are updated. Appendix C counts CRD/IFA parameters but omits fusion MLPs, grouping layers, classifiers, and other unfrozen parameters from a complete trainable-parameter comparison. The promised code link is blank.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Perturbation stability does not establish distribution-shift robustness, and separately fine-tuning models on two domains does not demonstrate robustness of one deployed model to a shift. Pathology claims rely on selected visualizations without expert validation or quantitative diagnostic evaluation; Appendix F's dismissal of glandular lumen relevance is also inadequately justified.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: making visual prompts interpretable through region-grounded, category-shared prototypes. Cross-layer grouping provides a useful mechanism for connecting fine and coarse concepts.

Reports encouraging results across five backbones on CUB. With DINOv2-B, IVPT achieves 90.8% accuracy and 75.3/75.9 consistency/stability, improving over the evaluated prototype-augmented prompting baselines.
Includes additional quantitative results on PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part, component and hierarchy ablations, extensive visualizations, and examples of failures involving background correlations.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification has unresolved problems. Equation 5 adds unconstrained spatial biases after softmax, so the resulting values need not be valid probabilities, despite their subsequent use in entropy and KL losses. Equation 8 applies KL divergence to hard-masked region maps without specifying normalization or handling mismatched zero supports. Equation 7 also leaves empty regions undefined. These details materially affect whether the stated objective is well-defined.

The central claim of faithful interpretation is insufficiently established. Pooling contextualized ViT features from a region does not ensure that its prediction depends only on that region. Consistency, stability, and cross-layer overlap assess localization and agreement, but no intervention or deletion experiments establish prediction faithfulness. Equation 4 also does not specify how class-score vectors become the normalized concept-importance values in Figure 5.

Novelty and comparisons are incomplete. PDiscoFormer supplies much of the part-discovery machinery but is not evaluated directly, and Prompt-CAM is discussed without an experimental comparison. The characterization of previous prototypes as necessarily class-specific overlooks the prototype-sharing literature cited by the paper. Matched comparisons are needed to isolate the contribution of interpretable prompting from established part discovery.

Evaluation protocols are insufficiently documented. The paper does not clearly explain how ordinary VPT prompts are converted into comparable region maps, how category-shared versus category-specific prototypes are scored, or the splits and part-label handling for the additional datasets. Main results lack repeated-run uncertainty, making small accuracy improvements difficult to assess.

Training and efficiency claims need reconciliation. The main text describes a frozen backbone with only prompt embeddings updated, whereas Appendix A also unfreezes positional embeddings and several backbone tokens. Appendix C counts CRD/IFA parameters but omits fusion MLPs, classifiers, and other trainable parameters. Consequently, total parameter efficiency and fairness relative to prompting baselines are not established.

The human study does not adequately support its strong conclusions. The reported 97.5% annotation accuracy is measured against undefined 'prototype intentions'; sampling, adjudication, participant expertise, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty, and baseline comparisons are missing. Likewise, separately fine-tuning models on different domains does not demonstrate robustness to deployment-time domain shifts.
